nodes.label: Middle Bronze city-states
nodes.full: Independent walled city-states — Hazor grew into the largest, ruling a substantial hinterland and named in the Mari archives as a major trading partner — each governed by their own local dynasty, with no single Canaanite state ever uniting the region even loosely before Egyptian conquest brought them under a shared, if distant, overlordship.
nodes.src: Hazor excavations, Yigael Yadin (1955–58, 1968) and later expeditions; Mari letters referencing Hazor.

nodes.label: Earthen ramparts
nodes.full: Canaanite cities of the Middle Bronze Age built massive sloped earthen ramparts, sometimes faced with stone or plaster, around their settlements — a fortification technology requiring an enormous, coordinated labour investment that produced defensive works some of which still dominate their sites' visible topography more than three and a half thousand years later.
nodes.src: Comparative Middle Bronze Age Levantine rampart construction, Hazor and other sites.

nodes.label: Wine and olive oil
nodes.full: Canaanite hill-country agriculture specialised in wine and olive oil beyond simple subsistence grain farming, producing surplus valuable enough to export by sea to Egypt and further afield — export commodities specific enough to this landscape that Egyptian texts recorded Canaanite wine and oil as recognisably distinct, desirable imports.
nodes.src: Comparative archaeobotanical and installation evidence (wine and olive presses) from Middle and Late Bronze Age Canaanite sites.

nodes.label: Canaanite temple architecture
nodes.full: Excavated temples at Hazor, Megiddo and other Canaanite cities show a recognisable regional architectural tradition — a long rectangular hall, often with a raised platform or niche for a cult statue at the far end — that later Israelite temple architecture, including the biblical description of Solomon's Temple, would draw on rather than invent from nothing.
nodes.src: Comparative Canaanite temple architecture, Hazor Area H temple and Megiddo temple remains.

nodes.label: Proto-Sinaitic script
nodes.full: Inscriptions left by Canaanite-speaking workers at Egyptian turquoise-mining sites in the Sinai adapted a small number of Egyptian hieroglyphic signs to represent the sounds of their own Semitic language — widely regarded as the earliest known alphabetic writing system and, transmitted through later Phoenician use, the ultimate ancestor of the Hebrew, Greek, Latin and Arabic alphabets alike.
nodes.src: Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions, Serabit el-Khadim, discovered by Flinders Petrie (1905).

nodes.label: Battle of Megiddo
nodes.full: Thutmose III's decisive victory over a coalition of Canaanite and Syrian rulers at Megiddo, recorded in unusually precise tactical detail on the walls of the Karnak temple, is the earliest battle in world history for which a reasonably detailed eyewitness-derived account survives — the opening campaign of nearly a century of intermittent Egyptian military presence in Canaan.
nodes.src: Annals of Thutmose III, Karnak Temple inscriptions.

nodes.label: Late Bronze Canaan under Egypt
nodes.full: Egyptian New Kingdom pharaohs reduced Canaan's city-kings to tribute-paying vassals after Thutmose III's conquests, garrisoning key towns while leaving local dynasties nominally in place — a light-touch imperial administration that the Amarna Letters reveal as prone to constant low-level rivalry and appeals to Egypt for support against neighbouring vassal kings.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters (EA 244–406, the Canaanite vassal correspondence); Egyptian New Kingdom topographical lists of conquered Canaanite towns.

nodes.label: Egyptian garrison administration
nodes.full: Egypt governed Canaan through a light administrative footprint — a few key garrison towns and an official ('the commissioner of northern lands') to oversee tribute collection — leaving most day-to-day rule in the hands of the existing local city-kings rather than replacing them with an Egyptian bureaucracy, a low-cost imperial model that also meant Egyptian control could be, and often was, locally contested.
nodes.src: Egyptian New Kingdom administrative titles and correspondence referencing Canaanite provincial oversight.

nodes.label: Vassal treaty obligations
nodes.full: Canaanite vassal kings' letters to Pharaoh consistently invoke formal obligations of loyalty and mutual military support in a recognisable treaty-relationship vocabulary, even where — as with Rib-Hadda of Byblos's dozens of increasingly desperate surviving letters — Egypt provided little of the promised protection in return.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters, Rib-Hadda of Byblos correspondence (EA 68–138, the largest single correspondent's archive).

nodes.label: Amarna vassal rivalries
nodes.full: Abdi-Heba, the Egyptian vassal ruler of Jerusalem, wrote repeatedly to Pharaoh Akhenaten complaining of attacks by neighbouring city-kings and by armed groups called Apiru, begging for Egyptian troops that mostly never came — correspondence that documents constant low-intensity warfare among Canaan's city-states even while all parties formally professed loyalty to the same Egyptian crown.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters, Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem correspondence (EA 285–290).

nodes.label: The Habiru
nodes.full: Amarna-era Canaanite vassal kings repeatedly complained to Pharaoh about raids and defections to bands called Apiru (Habiru) — a social category defined by statelessness and marginal legal status rather than by ethnicity, ranging from bandits to mercenaries to political refugees; the word's possible but historically disputed etymological connection to 'Hebrew' remains a live and unresolved scholarly question rather than an established fact.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters, Apiru references across multiple Canaanite vassal correspondents (e.g. EA 286–290); comparative scholarship on the disputed Habiru–Hebrew etymology.

nodes.label: Cuneiform diplomacy
nodes.full: Canaanite vassal kings corresponded with the Egyptian pharaoh in Akkadian cuneiform on clay tablets — the era's international diplomatic language — even though neither Canaan nor Egypt itself used cuneiform for everyday administration, evidence of a shared Near Eastern diplomatic culture that transcended any single empire's own script and language.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters archive, discovered at Akhetaten (Tell el-Amarna), 1887.

nodes.label: Great powers club
nodes.full: Egypt, the Hittite Empire, Babylon, Mitanni and Assyria addressed each other in Amarna-era diplomatic correspondence as equal 'brother' kings within a recognised international system, with smaller states like the Canaanite city-kingdoms occupying a distinctly lower, vassal-level rung — Canaan functioned as contested southern periphery to a genuine great-power order rather than a political centre of its own.
nodes.src: Amarna Letters, the 'Great Powers' correspondence between Egypt, Babylon, Mitanni, Assyria and Hatti (EA 1–44).

nodes.label: Ugarit golden age
nodes.full: The northern coastal city-state of Ugarit flourished as a genuinely cosmopolitan trading hub under nominal Hittite rather than Egyptian overlordship, its royal archive preserving an unusually rich body of administrative, diplomatic, legal and religious texts that make it one of the best-documented Bronze Age Levantine states by a wide margin.
nodes.src: Ras Shamra (Ugarit) excavations, Claude Schaeffer (1929 onward).

nodes.label: Ugaritic alphabetic cuneiform
nodes.full: Ugarit's scribes developed a separate, parallel alphabetic writing system of roughly thirty wedge-shaped cuneiform signs — genuinely alphabetic in structure despite its cuneiform appearance, but a distinct invention from the linear Proto-Sinaitic tradition that fed into Phoenician, illustrating that the alphabetic principle itself was independently discovered or adapted more than once in the Bronze Age Levant.
nodes.src: Ugaritic alphabetic cuneiform corpus, Ras Shamra archive.

nodes.label: Baal Cycle
nodes.full: Tablets from Ugarit's royal archive preserve the Baal Cycle, a mythological narrative of the storm-god Baal's conflicts with the sea-god Yam and death-god Mot — the fullest surviving textual window onto Canaanite religion's pantheon (El, Baal, Anat, Asherah among others), a tradition later biblical texts would polemicise against without ever fully erasing its cultural influence.
nodes.src: Baal Cycle tablets (KTU 1.1–1.6), Ugarit royal archive.

nodes.label: Epic of Kirta
nodes.full: Alongside the Baal Cycle, Ugarit's archive preserved narrative epic poetry — the Epic of Kirta, telling of a king's search for an heir with divine intervention — literary works of real sophistication that predate, and likely influenced in style and theme, comparable narrative poetry surviving from ancient Israel centuries later.
nodes.src: Epic of Kirta tablets (KTU 1.14–1.16), Ugarit royal archive.

nodes.label: Women property rights at Ugarit
nodes.full: Legal and economic tablets from Ugarit's archives record women, including some outside the royal family, holding, inheriting and transacting real property in their own name — direct documentary evidence of a defined legal capacity for women in Late Bronze Age Canaanite society, not merely an assumption read backward from later, less well-documented periods.
nodes.src: Ugaritic legal and economic tablet corpus, Ras Shamra archive.

nodes.label: Bronze and tin networks
nodes.full: Canaan's own copper resources needed tin, sourced from as far as Central Asia or possibly Cornwall via long relay trade chains, to make true bronze — a dependency that made Levantine coastal cities like Ugarit essential intermediary nodes in a Bronze Age metal-supply network stretching far beyond any single region's own natural resources.
nodes.src: Comparative tin-sourcing studies of Late Bronze Age eastern Mediterranean bronze artefacts.

nodes.label: Uluburun cargo
nodes.full: A Late Bronze Age merchant vessel that sank off the southern Anatolian coast carried Canaanite storage jars, Cypriot copper ingots, Egyptian gold, Mycenaean pottery, Baltic amber and African ebony in a single hold — physical proof that Canaan's coastal cities operated within a genuinely international Mediterranean and Near Eastern trade system spanning thousands of kilometres.
nodes.src: Uluburun shipwreck excavation, George Bass and Cemal Pulak (1984–94); Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology.

nodes.label: Megiddo ivories
nodes.full: A cache of carved ivory plaques and objects from a Late Bronze Age palace treasury at Megiddo, decorated with motifs drawn from Egyptian, Aegean and local Canaanite artistic traditions alike, shows the coastal Levant's role as a genuine meeting point of Bronze Age Mediterranean and Near Eastern visual culture rather than a passive recipient of any single tradition.
nodes.src: Megiddo ivory hoard, discovered 1937; Israel Museum, Jerusalem and Oriental Institute, University of Chicago.

nodes.label: Ugarit final letters
nodes.full: Among the last documents ever written at Ugarit, a letter from its king to the ruler of Cyprus describes an approaching hostile fleet and pleads for military assistance that, as the site's subsequent destruction and abandonment attests, never arrived in time — a first-person Bronze Age voice recorded at the very edge of the collapse that would end the whole Late Bronze Age system.
nodes.src: Ugarit's final tablet archive (RS 20.238 and related letters), found unbaked in the destruction layer.

nodes.label: Bronze Age collapse
nodes.full: Hazor, Ugarit and numerous other Late Bronze Age Levantine cities were destroyed or abandoned within a few decades around 1200 BC, alongside the collapse of the Hittite Empire and severe disruption to Egypt itself — a civilisational rupture whose causes (the 'Sea Peoples,' climate-driven drought, internal systems failure, or some combination) remain genuinely debated among specialists.
nodes.src: Destruction layers at Hazor and Ugarit; Ugarit's own final letters describing an approaching enemy fleet, likely its last surviving documents.

nodes.label: The collapse that ended an age
nodes.full: Within a single human generation the Hittite Empire disappeared, Egypt's New Kingdom empire in Canaan ended, and city after city across the eastern Mediterranean and Near East was destroyed or abandoned — one of history's most complete civilisational ruptures, whose end opened the political vacuum that Israelites, Philistines, Phoenicians and Aramaeans would fill across the following Iron Age.
nodes.src: Comparative Late Bronze Age Collapse scholarship across Anatolia, the Levant, Cyprus and the Aegean.
